questions.prompt: What does the row operation \(R_1\leftrightarrow R_3\) mean?
questions.answer: It means swap row \(1\) and row \(3\). No entries are changed except that the two complete rows exchange positions.

questions.prompt: What does \((A\mid\mathbf{b})\) represent for a system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\)?
questions.answer: It is the augmented matrix. The coefficient matrix \(A\) is written on the left of the vertical bar, and the right-hand-side vector \(\mathbf{b}\) is written as the column on the right of the bar.

questions.prompt: Write the augmented matrix for \(x+2y=7\), \(3x-y=4\).
questions.answer:
Use the variable order \((x,y)\). The first row is \((1,2\mid7)\), and the second row is \((3,-1\mid4)\). Thus
\[
\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&2&7\\3&-1&4\end{array}\right).
\]

questions.prompt: Is \(0R_2\) a valid row-scaling operation? Explain briefly.
questions.answer: No. Scaling a row is valid only when the multiplier is nonzero. Multiplying by \(0\) can erase an equation and change the solution set, so \(0R_2\) is not a valid elementary row operation.

questions.prompt: Apply \(R_2-2R_1\) to \(\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&8\\2&7&19\end{array}\right)\).
questions.answer:
Keep row \(1\) unchanged. Replace row \(2\) by row \(2\) minus \(2\) times row \(1\):
\[
(2,7,19)-2(1,3,8)=(0,1,3).
\]
The new matrix is
\[
\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&8\\0&1&3\end{array}\right).
\]

questions.prompt: Apply \(-\frac12 R_1\) to the first row of \(\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}-2&4&6\\1&0&5\end{array}\right)\).
questions.answer:
Multiply every entry of row \(1\), including the augmented entry, by \(-\frac12\):
\[
-\frac12(-2,4,6)=(1,-2,-3).
\]
Row \(2\) is unchanged, so the result is
\[
\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&-2&-3\\1&0&5\end{array}\right).
\]

questions.prompt: Use one row operation to make the lower-left entry zero in \(\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}2&1&5\\6&4&16\end{array}\right)\).
questions.answer:
The lower-left entry \(6\) is \(3\) times the pivot entry \(2\). Use \(R_2-3R_1\):
\[
(6,4,16)-3(2,1,5)=(0,1,1).
\]
The result is
\[
\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}2&1&5\\0&1&1\end{array}\right).
\]

questions.prompt: The first row of an augmented matrix is \((1,-2\mid4)\), and the second row is \((3,1\mid5)\). Compute the new second row after \(R_2-3R_1\).
questions.answer:
Apply the operation to the complete augmented row:
\[
(3,1,5)-3(1,-2,4)=(3-3,1+6,5-12).
\]
So the new second row is
\[
(0,7\mid -7).
\]

questions.prompt: Starting from \(\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&2&9\\3&5&22\end{array}\right)\), use row operations to solve the represented system.
questions.answer:
Use \(R_2-3R_1\):
\[
(3,5,22)-3(1,2,9)=(0,-1,-5).
\]
So the second row gives \(-y=-5\), hence \(y=5\). The first row gives
\[
x+2y=9.
\]
Substitute \(y=5\):
\[
x+10=9,
\]
so \(x=-1\). The solution is \((-1,5)\).

questions.prompt: Convert \(2x-y+z=3\), \(-x+4z=8\), \(y-z=-2\) into an augmented matrix using variable order \((x,y,z)\).
questions.answer:
List coefficients in the order \((x,y,z)\). The equations give rows \((2,-1,1\mid3)\), \((-1,0,4\mid8)\), and \((0,1,-1\mid-2)\). Therefore the augmented matrix is
\[
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c}2&-1&1&3\\-1&0&4&8\\0&1&-1&-2\end{array}\right).
\]

questions.prompt: Explain why \(R_i+cR_j\) preserves the solution set when \(i\ne j\).
questions.answer: If a variable tuple satisfies both original rows \(R_i\) and \(R_j\), then it also satisfies the equation formed by \(R_i+cR_j\), because adding \(c\) times a true equation to another true equation gives a true equation. The operation is reversible: subtract \(cR_j\) from the new row to recover the old \(R_i\). Since the step can be undone, it does not add or remove solutions.

questions.prompt: A row operation changes only the coefficient entries but leaves the augmented entry unchanged. Explain why this is invalid.
questions.answer: An augmented row represents a whole equation, including its right-hand side. A row operation must be applied to every entry in the row. If the coefficients are changed but the augmented entry is not changed consistently, the new row may represent a different equation that is not equivalent to the original system. This can change the \(solution\) set.

questions.prompt: Find a sequence of row operations that changes \(\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}0&2&6\\1&3&8\end{array}\right)\) into a form with a leading \(1\) in the first row, first column.
questions.answer:
The first entry of row \(1\) is zero, so swap the two rows:
\[
R_1\leftrightarrow R_2.
\]
This gives
\[
\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&8\\0&2&6\end{array}\right).
\]
Now the first row, first column contains a leading \(1\), as required.

questions.prompt: Use row operations to transform \(\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}2&4&10\\1&3&7\end{array}\right)\) so the first column is \((1,0)^T\).
questions.answer:
First swap rows to use the existing \(1\) as the pivot:
\[
\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&7\\2&4&10\end{array}\right).
\]
Then use \(R_2-2R_1\):
\[
(2,4,10)-2(1,3,7)=(0,-2,-4).
\]
The transformed matrix is
\[
\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&3&7\\0&-2&-4\end{array}\right).
\]

questions.prompt: For which values of \(k\) is scaling row \((k,2\mid5)\) by \(\frac1k\) a valid row operation?
questions.answer:
Scaling by \(\frac1k\) is valid only when the scalar exists and is nonzero. The number \(\frac1k\) exists only if \(k\ne0\). When \(k\ne0\), \(\frac1k\) is also nonzero. Therefore the operation is valid exactly for
\[
k\ne0.
\]

questions.prompt: The row \((0,a\mid6)\) is obtained after row operations. Classify the information it gives for \(a=0\) and for \(a\ne0\).
questions.answer:
If \(a=0\), the row is
\[
(0,0\mid6),
\]
which represents \(0=6\). That is inconsistent, so the system has no solution. If \(a\ne0\), the row represents
\[
ay=6,
\]
so it determines
\[
y=\frac6a.
\]
Thus \(a=0\) gives a contradiction, while \(a\ne0\) gives a pivot equation for \(y\).

questions.prompt: Choose \(c\) so that applying \(R_2+cR_1\) to rows \((2,-1\mid4)\) and \((5,3\mid7)\) makes the first entry of row \(2\) zero.
questions.answer:
The new first entry of row \(2\) is
\[
5+c\cdot2.
\]
Set it equal to zero:
\[
5+2c=0.
\]
Then
\[
c=-\frac52.
\]
So the operation is \(R_2-\frac52R_1\).

questions.prompt: Diagnose the error: after \(R_2-2R_1\), a learner changes \((2,3\mid9)\), \((4,7\mid20)\) into \((2,3\mid9)\), \((0,1\mid20)\).
questions.answer:
The coefficients were updated but the augmented entry was not. The complete second row should be
\[
(4,7,20)-2(2,3,9)=(0,1,2).
\]
So the correct result is
\[
(2,3\mid9),\qquad (0,1\mid2).
\]
Leaving \(20\) unchanged changes the represented equation and can change the solution set.

questions.prompt: Prove that swapping two rows is reversible and therefore preserves the solution set.
questions.answer: Swapping rows \(i\) and \(j\) only changes the order in which the equations are written. If the same swap is applied again, row \(i\) returns to its original position and row \(j\) returns to its original position. Thus the operation is its own inverse. Since no equation is altered and the step can be undone exactly, the set of variable values satisfying all rows is unchanged.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to replace \(R_1\) by \(R_1+2R_1\) and calls it an add-multiple row operation. Is this valid, and what standard operation is it equivalent to?
questions.answer:
The standard operation \(R_i+cR_j\) uses another row \(j\) with \(i\ne j\). Here the learner is combining row \(1\) with itself:
\[
R_1+2R_1=3R_1.
\]
This is not an add-multiple operation using a different row, but it is equivalent to scaling row \(1\) by \(3\). Since \(3\ne0\), that scaling operation is valid and preserves the solution set.
